title: GPU lane saturation and host staging notes
content:
Purpose:

This is a working log of a set of experiments exploring a specific multi-GPU performance class: what happens when inter-GPU lanes (NVLink / PCIe / host) get saturated by small, frequent transfers (microbursts) during LLM inference. The aim is to identify practical knobs in the runtime (streaming, host staging, NCCL config, batching heuristics) to reduce p50/p95/p99 tail and improve cost-effective throughput.

Context / Motivation:
- We've seen production traces where 8-GPU inference pods show good median latency but significant p99 spikes for short requests (seq_len < 64, batch 1-4).
- Hypothesis: many small kernels + small host-device transfers + synchronous host staging create microbursts that saturate PCIe/host bandwidth and cause queueing in NCCL/NVLink.
- This doc captures reproducible tests, profiling artefacts, and a set of recommended runtime adjustments.

Hardware and software baseline:
- Test rigs: 2 node DGX-like setups (4xA100 40GB NVLink per node) and 1-node H100 8xNVLink (cloud instance equivalent).
- OS/driver: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.2, NVIDIA drivers 535.x, NCCL 2.18, UCX disabled (we used default CUDA IPC / nvlink paths).
- Runtime: serving-runtime main@commit a4c9b2f (local perf branch), model: quantized decoder-only transformer ~20B tokens embedding kv-cache usage.
- Measurement tools: nvprof/ncu for kernels, nvtx ranges, perf top for host, nvidia-smi dmon for link counters, nccl-tests (all_reduce/all_gather) for baseline comm throughput.

Experiment 1 — microburst emulation (small transfers):
- Workload: generate sequences where the model emits tokens in bursts of 4 tokens with 20ms think time between bursts (simulate streaming generation with function calls).
- Metric: request latency distribution, NCCL wait times (from nvtx), PCIe transfer queue depth, host memory copy throughput.

Observations:
- High p99 correlated with host->device memcopy spikes: short cudaMemcpyAsync calls (2–16KB ranges) serialized on the host when pinned buffers were exhausted.
- nvlink utilization remained moderate, but PCIe (to NVLink bridge) and host CPU copy activity showed bursts that aligned with tail events.
- NCCL showed short (5–15ms) stalls where collective progress stalled waiting on data availability; these stalls weren't long enough to look catastrophic in isolation but caused queueing for subsequent requests.

Experiment 2 — pinned buffer pool sizing and staging strategies:
- Tests: varying a pre-allocated pinned host buffer pool size (16MB, 64MB, 256MB) and switching between single-threaded staging loop vs. a small thread-pool for host-to-device enqueues.

Results:
- Small pool (16MB): frequent buffer exhaustion -> host memcpy fallbacks -> synchronous copies -> tail latency spikes up to 4x median.
- Medium pool (64MB): big improvement on p95, but occasional spikes remained under high concurrency (n > 12).
- Large pool (256MB): stable p99 for our test load, but memory pressure on nodes increased noticeably.
- Threaded staging: decoupling host copy submission from main request thread reduced blocking in request-path and improved p99 by ~30% compared to inline staging.

Implication: allocate a modest pinned buffer pool per-worker (default 64–128MB) and use a small staging thread-pool to batch small transfers into fewer device enqueues.

Experiment 3 — CUDA streams per-GPU and kernel overlap:
- Setup: vary streams per-GPU (1, 2, 4, 8) for asynchronous kernels and memcpy overlaps. Use nvtx to observe overlap.

Findings:
- Single stream: kernels and memcopies serialized; no overlap -> worst tail.
- 2–4 streams: good overlap for our kernels (reduced idle gaps on GPU SMs) and lower queuing on PCIe. 8 streams showed diminishing returns and increased scheduling overhead on host.

Guidance: default to 2–4 streams per GPU for inference threads. Dynamically reduce stream count for very small sequence lengths where kernel runtime << transfer time to avoid context switching overhead.

Experiment 4 — NCCL algorithm and hierarchy sensitivity:
- We toggled NCCL_COLLNET, tree/ring algorithms where available, and measured p99 under skewed GPU topologies (islanded NVLink groups: two pairs connected via PCIe).

Results:
- For fully connected NVLink topologies, COLLNET lowered p99 at high concurrency by removing PCIe hops.
- In islanded setups, tree algorithms that minimized cross-island collectives outperformed naive ring: choose algorithm based on topology and request size.

Practical runtime knobs explored and effects:
- NCCL_P2P_LEVEL / NCCL_ALGO: force tree/collnet for topology-aware runs. Reduced cross-node tail events by ~20%.
- Batching heuristic: delay-first-token by a short adaptive window (2–6ms) to coalesce immediate small requests. Increased median by ~5% but reduced p99 by ~35% for bursty workloads.
- KV prefetch coalescing: group KV cache fetches for next-token beamlets into contiguous device transfers. Very effective for small-seq models.
- Adaptive pinned pool scaling: grow/shrink based on recent allocation rate. Helps control memory while avoiding exhaustion.

Quick config recommendation (starting point):
- pinned_pool_per_worker: 96MB
- staging_threads: 2
- cuda_streams_per_gpu: 3
- nccl_algo_hint: topology-aware (collnet if full NVLink, tree otherwise)
- coalesce_window_ms: adaptive, default 3ms (disable for latency-critical single-shot requests)

Open questions / follow-ups:
- UCX vs CUDA IPC vs nvlink: we disabled UCX for simplicity. Need a controlled comparison because UCX offloads some progress semantics and may change host CPU patterns.
- Host CPU core pinning: some stalls looked like scheduling jitter; experiment with pinning staging threads to isolated cores.
- Microbenchmark to quantify threshold where coalescing hurts median. Need a simple synthesizer to map sequence length, batch, and token emission gap to optimal coalesce_window_ms.
- Interaction with quantization kernels: smaller kernels have different scheduling behavior; replicate experiments with int8 kernels.

Immediate action items (short list):
- (Priya) implement pinned pool + staging thread-pool in perf branch and run 72-hour soak on H100 cloud nodes (ticket ENG-7893).
- (Ethan) add topology detection and NCCL hinting in config layer (PR #412).
- (Leah) generate synthetic workload matrix and run grid to find coalesce window sweet spots for common models.

Notes to self (rough):
- When reading nvtx traces: look for repeated small memcpy ranges clustered tightly before NCCL op start -> signature of microburst.
- If PCIe dmon shows steady high link utilization then it's a sustained bandwidth problem; if spikes align with requests then it's queuing/microburst.

Appendix — quick nvprof/nvtx snippet:
- nvtx ranges: push("stage:host-memcpy") / push("kernel:attn") / push("nccl:allgather")
- env opts we used: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, NCCL_ALGO=tree, NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=NVL, CUDA_STREAM_PER_THREAD=1
- sample command: ./bin/serving-runtime --trace-nvtx --pinned-pool-size=96MB --staging-threads=2 --coalesce-ms=3

End — high level take: microbursts from small host-device transfers + limited pinned buffer capacity are a common cause of p99 tail in multi-GPU inference. A combination of modest pinned pools, lightweight staging threads, stream tuning, and topology-aware NCCL hints gives large practical wins with little model change.

If others want to replicate, ping me and I'll hand over the exact perf branch and cloud instance types used.
